title: Support for Democracy—but also Strongmen—Is Rising in Latin America
gist: The 2026 AmericasBarometer (25,282 interviews across 21 countries) finds support for democracy in Latin America up six points to 65%, the first broad upturn in a generation—but the rebound is driven by improved economic conditions and delivery, not by commitment to liberal norms. Meanwhile trust in China (51%) has overtaken trust in the U.S. (40%), a reversal from 57% vs. 62% a decade ago.

themes.theme: Democracy rebound is performance-based, not norm-based

insights.claim: Sixty-five percent of Latin Americans now say democracy is better than any other form of government, six points above 2023, with gains in nearly every country and across every age and education group—the first broad upturn in a generation.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: A regional legitimacy floor reduces near-term tail risk of disorderly regime rupture, but because the driver is cyclical it is not a structural de-risking of LatAm political risk premia.
insights.quote: Sixty-five percent of Latin Americans now agree that democracy, whatever its problems, is better than any other form of government, six points higher than in 2023.
insights.locator: After more than a decade of steady erosion

insights.claim: Support for democracy in Latin America is contingent on two factors—governments delivering concrete results and an economy providing opportunity—so a growth or delivery shock should be expected to reverse the 2026 gains.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Treat the democracy rebound as a coincident indicator of the LatAm cycle: a regional growth downturn is likely to be followed by renewed institutional stress and populist outcomes.
insights.quote: much public support for democracy is contingent on two key factors: the government delivering concrete results and the economy providing greater opportunity
insights.locator: Second, much public support for democracy

insights.claim: Support based on appreciation for civil liberties is durable while support based on economic performance is fragile—and the 2023-2026 rise in Latin American support for democracy came mostly from the fragile, performance-based channel.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: A usable mental model for pricing political durability: distinguish rights-anchored legitimacy (sticky) from delivery-anchored legitimacy (mean-reverting with the business cycle).
insights.quote: support for democracy based on appreciation for civil liberties is durable, while support based on economic performance is more fragile
insights.locator: In other words, support for democracy based on

insights.claim: Citizens who credit democracy with protecting freedoms better than past authoritarian regimes are consistently more likely to reject censorship, one-party rule and executives who override courts, while those who credit democracy only with better economic growth are barely more committed than those who credit it with nothing.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Identifies which national publics will actually resist executive overreach—an early-warning screen for where rule-of-law risk to contracts and property is highest.
insights.locator: Memories of authoritarianism

themes.theme: Illiberal majoritarianism decoupled from pro-democracy sentiment

insights.claim: Across Latin America, respondents' stated support for 'democracy' had virtually no correlation with their answers to seven questions about core democratic norms, meaning headline democracy-support polling is not a proxy for institutional strength.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Discount pro-democracy survey headlines as evidence of institutional safety; price checks-and-balances risk off separate indicators like judicial independence and term-limit changes.
insights.quote: Respondents’ support for “democracy” had virtually no correlation with how they felt about these core pillars of democratic systems.
insights.locator: Support for democracy is only weakly connected

insights.claim: Across the region illiberal majoritarians—those favoring fewer checks on executive power—are more, not less, likely to say they support democracy, inverting the relationship democratic theory predicts.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Electorates may reward, not punish, executives who dismantle judicial and legislative constraints—raising the probability of policy volatility and expropriation-style risk even in popular governments.
insights.locator: Yet across the region, illiberal majoritarians

insights.claim: In El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Honduras and Guatemala, more than 60% of citizens score on the upper half of an 'illiberal majoritarianism' scale favoring fewer checks and balances, especially on executive power.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Names the four markets where public opinion supplies political cover for executive-power concentration—relevant to sovereign, concession and regulatory risk in Central America and the Caribbean.
insights.locator: In El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Honduras

insights.claim: Only in Chile, Argentina and Uruguay does support for democracy track support for civil liberties, separation of powers and minority protections the way democratic theory predicts.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: The Southern Cone trio retains a genuine societal constraint on executive overreach—an underappreciated differentiator for long-horizon institutional risk pricing versus the rest of the region.
insights.locator: Only in Chile, Argentina, and Uruguay

themes.theme: El Salvador as the template: security delivery buys legitimacy

insights.claim: Salvadorans are the region's most supportive of illiberal majoritarianism, and a majority there believes the country's last authoritarian regime respected civil liberties more than the current government—yet they broadly back that government and increasingly say they support democracy.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Demonstrates voters will knowingly trade civil liberties for outcomes, so security-first governments face little domestic electoral constraint—lowering the odds of policy reversal but raising rule-of-law risk.
insights.locator: El Salvador is the clearest case

insights.claim: El Salvador combines the hemisphere's lowest crime victimization rate at 8% with the region's highest presidential approval at 83%, and support for democracy there rose a full seven points from 2023 to 2026.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Quantifies the security-for-approval trade that other LatAm candidates will campaign on; expect the Bukele security model to be replicated and to shape 2026-2028 election platforms region-wide.

insights.claim: To Salvadoran respondents, winning elections and delivering results alone confer democratic legitimacy, and anything constraining a popular president is treated as an obstacle to democracy rather than a safeguard.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Explains why courts, term limits and opposition parties provide weak protection for investors in high-approval regimes—legal constraints can be dismantled with popular consent.

themes.theme: China overtakes the U.S. on regional trust

insights.claim: Trust in the U.S. government across Latin America has fallen to 40% while trust in China has risen to 51%, reversing a decade-ago position of 62% U.S. versus 57% China.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: A 22-point swing in relative trust is a leading indicator for Chinese market access in LatAm infrastructure, ports, telecom and critical minerals—and for political tolerance of Chinese capital over U.S. alternatives.
insights.quote: Today, China has a wide lead: Only 40% trust the U.S., versus 51% for China.
insights.locator: Today, China has a wide lead

insights.claim: In Mexico 55% trust China versus 23% for the United States, and in Haiti the figures are 73% and 40%, with the U.S. still ahead only in Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic and Honduras.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Mexico's 32-point trust gap against the U.S. is a domestic political constraint on Washington-aligned nearshoring and security policy, and a tailwind for Chinese investment despite USMCA pressure.
insights.quote: In Mexico, 55% trust China and 23% trust the United States. In Haiti, it’s 73% and 40%.
insights.locator: In Mexico, 55% trust China

themes.theme: Material conditions improving across the region

insights.claim: Since 2023 the share of Latin Americans saying their economy has worsened has fallen in 14 of 16 countries surveyed.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Broad-based improvement in household economic perception supports consumption-linked LatAm equities and incumbent re-election odds heading into the 2026-2027 electoral calendar.
insights.locator: First, the warming seems to reflect improvements

insights.claim: Regional food insecurity has eased from a pandemic peak of one-third of the population to just over one-quarter, and the share feeling unsafe in their own neighborhood fell from 49% to 40%.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the post-pandemic cost-of-living and crime shocks have partly unwound—supportive of discretionary spending and of political stability, but reversible if inflation returns.
insights.locator: Food insecurity eased from a pandemic peak

themes.theme: Institutional erosion continues despite the mood shift

insights.claim: The regional uptick in pro-democracy sentiment is occurring alongside concrete institutional rollbacks: Nicaragua announcing it will cease holding elections, El Salvador scrapping presidential term limits, Mexico electing its entire federal judiciary on 13% turnout, and Peru swearing in its ninth president in a decade.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Public sentiment and institutional quality have decoupled, so investors relying on polling or approval ratings as governance proxies will systematically underprice legal and contract risk in these four markets.
insights.quote: Nicaragua has announced it would cease holding elections, El Salvador has scrapped presidential term limits, Mexico has elected its entire federal judiciary with only 13% participation, and Peru has sworn in its ninth president in a decade.
insights.locator: Paradoxical gains

insights.claim: Large majorities of Latin Americans associate democracy favorably with a system in which an elected president can act without obstacles, sidelining the opposition, the judiciary and minority rights.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Judicial independence and minority protections lack a popular constituency in most of the region—raising the base rate of court-packing, judicial elections and emergency-power regimes.
insights.quote: a system in which an elected president can get things done without obstacles, sidelining political opposition, the judiciary, and minority rights
insights.locator: Large majorities of Latin Americans associate

themes.theme: The U.S. and Canada as outliers on democratic commitment

insights.claim: Asked to choose between a system guaranteeing fair elections and one guaranteeing income and basic services, the U.S. and Canada rank last of the 20 countries surveyed, with only 46% and 35% respectively choosing elections, while Haiti (84%) and Peru (77%) rank highest.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: North American publics are the most willing in the hemisphere to trade electoral guarantees for material security—an underpriced input to U.S. and Canadian political risk and to the durability of redistributive policy platforms.
insights.quote: the U.S. and Canada rank last among the 20 countries surveyed, with only 46% and 35%, respectively, choosing elections
insights.locator: This is far from just a Latin American problem

insights.claim: Majorities of both Democrats and Republicans in the United States would take guaranteed income and basic services over guaranteed fair elections, making the preference bipartisan rather than a partisan artifact.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Cross-partisan demand for material guarantees points to durable fiscal expansion pressure in the U.S. regardless of which party holds power—relevant to long-duration Treasury positioning.
insights.quote: Majorities of both Democrats and Republicans would take the guaranteed income.
insights.locator: Majorities of both Democrats and Republicans

insights.claim: Democratic commitment is not a function of how rich or how consolidated a democracy is, but of what citizens believe democracy is currently doing for them.
insights.speaker: NOAM LUPU
insights.so_what: Removes GDP per capita and democratic vintage as safe proxies for institutional durability—developed-market political risk should be modeled on delivery, not on history.
insights.quote: Clearly, democratic commitment is not a function of how rich or how consolidated a democracy is.
